cards.explanation: The answer is that the number keeps on growing. Verse 14 says, “Yet more and more believers were brought to the Lord…” and that means large numbers of both men and women. Even with others holding back from joining, the number keeps climbing. That's a crowd that needs a bigger tray every time you turn around, friends.

The answer is Peter's shadow. Verse 15 says people laid the sick on cots and mats “…so that at least Peter’s shadow might fall on some of them as he passed…” Peter is one of the apostles, and they're hoping for at least his shadow. When the hope is that small and still that bold, I think folks believed something big was going on.

The answer is True! Verse 16 says crowds gathered from the towns around Jerusalem, bringing the sick and those tormented by unclean spirits, “…and all of them were healed.” All of them, friends. Not most, not some. That's like pulling out the whole batch and every single cookie came out perfect.

The answer is that they arrest the apostles and put them in jail. Verses 17 and 18 say the high priest and his associates, who belonged to the party of the Sadducees, were filled with jealousy. They went out, arrested the apostles and put them in the public jail. Jealousy rarely sends anybody out to bake a batch of anything good.

The answer is angel! Verse 19 says during the night “…an angel of the Lord opened the doors of the jail and brought them out…” An angel of the Lord is the one who called me out of the junk drawer I'd been stuck in for years, so I'm a big fan. Locked doors don't stop the Lord's messengers.

The answer is to go tell the full message of new life in the temple courts. The angel says, “Go, stand in the temple courts and tell the people the full message of this new life.” The apostles walk out of jail and are sent straight to the temple courts. That's not a quiet instruction, friends. It's a LOUD one.

The answer is False. The officers report, “We found the jail securely locked, with the guards posted at the doors; but when we opened them, we found no one inside.” So the doors were not broken open. Locked tight, nothing broken, and nobody home. That's a report nobody wants to hand a boss.

The answer is perplexed, the word in verse 24. The captain of the temple guard and the chief priests hear that the jail was locked and guarded and the apostles were gone, and they don't know what's happening. I'd be perplexed too, friends. I can lose a spatula in a kitchen this small.

The answer is False. Verse 26 says the captain and the officers brought the apostles, but not by force. So the apostles were not dragged in. The text gives the reason: they feared the people would stone them.

The answer is that they fear the people will stone them. Verse 26 says they brought the apostles in “…but not by force, for fear the people would stone them.” The people regarded the apostles highly (verse 13), and the captain had that crowd to think about.

The answer is that the apostles are determined to make the Council responsible for this man's blood. The high priest says they are “…determined to make us responsible for this man’s blood.” He means Jesus, the man they've been teaching about. It's the one complaint he saves for last.

The answer is to obey God rather than men. Peter and the other apostles say, “We must obey God rather than men.” That's the whole answer, friends. They'd just heard the high priest's strict orders, and they point to a higher voice.

The answer is to grant Israel repentance and forgiveness. The apostles say God exalted Jesus to His right hand as Prince and Savior, “…in order to grant repentance and forgiveness of sins to Israel.” Notice what's on the table: forgiveness. They say that to the same Council that was ready to shut them up.

The answer is True! The apostles say, “We are witnesses of these things, and so is the Holy Spirit, whom God has given to those who obey Him.” So they stand there as witnesses, and they say the Holy Spirit is one too. That's a witness list with a very special name on it.

The answer is outside. Verse 34 says Gamaliel, a Pharisee and a teacher of the law, “…ordered that the men be put outside for a short time.” That gives him a moment to speak to the Council about the apostles without them in the room.

The answer is False. Gamaliel says Judas the Galilean appeared in the days of the census and drew people after him, but he perished, “…and all his followers were scattered.” They didn't stay together, friends.

The answer is fail. Gamaliel says, “…if their purpose or endeavor is of human origin, it will fail.” He had just reminded the Council of Theudas and Judas the Galilean, whose followers scattered. His advice is to leave the apostles alone and let them go.

The answer is fighting against God. Gamaliel says, “But if it is from God, you will not be able to stop them. You may even find yourselves fighting against God.” That's a pretty serious thing to tell a room that was just enraged.

The answer is True. Verse 40 says the Council had the apostles flogged and ordered them not to speak in the name of Jesus. Then it says they “released them.” I think that's a hard verse to read, friends, so let's say it plainly. The apostles were let go.

The answer is rejoicing. Verse 41 says the apostles left the Sanhedrin “…rejoicing that they had been counted worthy of suffering disgrace for the Name.” After a flogging, that's a surprising thing to read. I think it shows how much the Name meant to them.

The answer is False. Verse 42 says that every day, in the temple courts and from house to house, “…they did not stop teaching and proclaiming the good news that Jesus is the Christ.” So they did not stop teaching in the temple courts. The order didn't stop them, friends.
